newsitem.title: USA: Japan's former Peru envoy says he is not 'scapegoat'.
newsitem.headline: Japan's former Peru envoy says he is not 'scapegoat'.

text.p: Japan's former ambassador to Peru said he is not his government's scapegoat for the four-month hostage crisis at his residence in Lima and that he has no regrets because "I did my best."

"I'm not a scapegoat of my government. But I may be a scapegoat for Japanese public opinion," said Morihisa Aoki, in an interview with the current issue of Newsweek International, which goes on sale on Monday.

Aoki, whose residence was taken over by Marxist rebels during a cocktail party on Dec. 17, has come under fire in Peru and in Japan since the crisis ended on April 22 when Peruvian troops stormed the house and freed the captives.
There were reports that Aoki ignored security warnings ahead of the party. Some former hostages have also been quoted anonymously as saying he was arrogant and drank too much.

"If the Japanese people can believe the crisis happened because there was a stupid ambassador throwing an unnecessary party, ignoring all risks and dangers, then they don't have to emerge from their lukewark bath of pacifism and inward-looking habits," Aoki told Newsweek, in an interview in Tokyo.
But he added, "If people believe that because I got kicked out there won't be any more crises for Japan, they're wrong."
Aoki said he offered his resignation but Japan's foreign minister did not accept it. He was relieved of his post in Peru, but remains ambassador at large, pending a final decision by the government.
Asked about reports he had turned down an offer from the Peruvian government of extra security for the party, Aoki said, "That is a propaganda campaign by the Peruvian police."

"If the Peruvian government really had some hint (of an attack), why then did two cabinet ministers, the (brother) of the president, and, above all, the top people of the anti-terrorist bureau of the Peruvian police attend the party," he said. "There was no such request by the Peruvian police to strengthen our security measures."
Aoki said he had been in touch with his fellow hostages and that he was not on friendly terms with all of them but that "many people have called me on the telephone or even visited me."
He said he had no regrets about his actions. "It's a bit awkward for me to say, but I couldn't have done better," he said. "I did my best."
